mn79:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.
mn79:1.3: Now on that occasion Sakuludāyī the Wanderer was staying in the Wanderers’ Park, the Peacocks’ Sanctuary, together with a large assembly of wanderers.
mn79:2.1: Then when it was morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, he went into Rājagaha for alms.
mn79:2.3: ‘It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha.
mn79:2.4: Suppose I went to Sakuludāyī the Wanderer in the Wanderers’ Park, the Peacocks’ Sanctuary?’
mn79:2.5: Then the Blessed One went to the Wanderers’ Park, the Peacocks’ Sanctuary.
mn79:3.1: Now on that occasion Sakuludāyī the Wanderer was sitting together with a large assembly of wanderers who were shouting and making a great uproar and noise, talking many kinds of pointless talk, such as:
mn79:3.2: talk of kings, talk of robbers, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of battles, talk of food, talk of drink, talk of clothes, talk of beds, talk of garlands, talk of scents, talk of relatives, talk of vehicles, talk of villages, talk of towns, talk of cities, talk of countries, talk of women, talk of heroes, talk of streets, talk of wells, talk of the departed, various idle tales, speculation about the world, speculation about the sea, talk of whether things are or are not, and so on.
mn79:3.3: Sakuludāyī the Wanderer saw the Blessed One coming in the distance.
mn79:3.4: Seeing him, he quieted his own assembly:
mn79:3.5: “Be quiet, sirs, do not make a noise.
mn79:3.7: that venerable one likes quiet and speaks in praise of quiet.
mn79:3.8: Perhaps, finding our assembly quiet, he will think it fit to approach.”
mn79:4.1: Then the Blessed One went up to Sakuludāyī the Wanderer.
mn79:4.2: Sakuludāyī the Wanderer said to the Blessed One:
mn79:4.3: “Let the Blessed One come, venerable sir.
mn79:4.4: Welcome to the Blessed One, venerable sir.
mn79:4.5: It is long, venerable sir, since the Blessed One made an occasion to come here.
mn79:4.6: Let the Blessed One be seated, venerable sir;
mn79:4.8: The Blessed One sat down on the seat made ready.
mn79:4.9: And Sakuludāyī the Wanderer took a certain low seat and sat down at one side.
mn79:4.10: The Blessed One then said to Sakuludāyī the Wanderer, as he sat at one side:
mn79:4.11: “What talk are you gathered here for now, Udāyī? And what was your discussion that was left unfinished?”
mn79:5.1: “Let that be, venerable sir, this talk for which we are now gathered here.
mn79:5.2: It will not be hard for the Blessed One to hear about it later too, venerable sir.
mn79:5.3: Venerable sir, when I have not come to this assembly, it sits talking many kinds of pointless talk;
mn79:5.4: but when I have come to this assembly, it sits looking only at my face, thinking:
mn79:5.5: ‘Let us hear the Dhamma that the ascetic Udāyī will speak’;
mn79:5.6: and when the Blessed One has come to this assembly, then both I and this assembly sit looking at the Blessed One’s face, thinking:
mn79:5.7: ‘Let us hear the Dhamma that the Blessed One will speak.’”
mn79:6.1: “Well then, Udāyī, let it occur to you to speak of that, in whatever way it may occur to you.”
mn79:6.2: “A few days ago, venerable sir—there was one who claimed to be omniscient and all-seeing, professing complete knowledge and vision thus: ‘Whether I am walking or standing, asleep or awake, knowledge and vision are continuously and unceasingly present to me.’
mn79:6.3: When I asked him a question about the past, he evaded it with another question, turned the talk aside to something outside the point, and displayed anger, hatred, and sulkiness.
mn79:6.4: Then, venerable sir, I became mindful only of the Blessed One:
mn79:6.5: ‘Ah, surely it is the Blessed One, surely it is the Fortunate One, who is thoroughly skilled in these things.’”
mn79:6.6: “But, Udāyī, who was that who claimed to be omniscient and all-seeing, professing complete knowledge and vision thus: ‘Whether I am walking or standing, asleep or awake, knowledge and vision are continuously and unceasingly present to me’, who, when you asked him a question about the past, evaded it with another question, turned the talk aside to something outside the point, and displayed anger, hatred, and sulkiness?”
mn79:7.1: “Udāyī, if someone were to recollect his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births … thus with their aspects and particulars, were to recollect his manifold past lives, then either he might ask me a question about the past, or I might ask him a question about the past;
mn79:7.2: and either he might satisfy my mind with his answer to a question about the past, or I might satisfy his mind with my answer to a question about the past.
mn79:7.3: And, Udāyī, if someone, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, were to see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings pass on according to their actions, then either he might ask me a question about the future, or I might ask him a question about the future;
mn79:7.4: and either he might satisfy my mind with his answer to a question about the future, or I might satisfy his mind with my answer to a question about the future.
mn79:7.5: But, Udāyī, let the past be, let the future be.
mn79:7.6: I shall teach you the Dhamma:
mn79:7.7: when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises;
mn79:7.8: when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.”
mn79:8.1: “Venerable sir, I am not even able to recollect with its aspects and particulars all that I have experienced in this very existence,[^1]
mn79:8.2: so how could I recollect my manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births … with their aspects and particulars, as the Blessed One does?
mn79:8.3: Indeed, venerable sir, I cannot even see a dust-goblin right now,
mn79:8.4: so how could I, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings pass on according to their actions, as the Blessed One does?
mn79:8.5: But when the Blessed One said to me:
mn79:8.6: ‘But, Udāyī, let the past be, let the future be;
mn79:8.7: I shall teach you the Dhamma:
mn79:8.8: when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises;
mn79:8.9: when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases’—that is even more unclear to me.
mn79:8.10: Perhaps, venerable sir, an answer to a question about our own teacher’s doctrine might satisfy the Blessed One’s mind.”
mn79:9.1: “Well, Udāyī, what is it in your own teacher’s doctrine?”
mn79:9.2: “Venerable sir, in our own teacher’s doctrine it is thus:
mn79:9.3: ‘This is the highest splendour, this is the highest splendour.’”
mn79:9.4: “But, Udāyī, since in your own teacher’s doctrine it is thus:
mn79:9.5: ‘This is the highest splendour, this is the highest splendour’—what is that highest splendour?”
mn79:9.6: “Venerable sir, that splendour than which there is no other splendour higher or more excellent—that is the highest splendour.”
mn79:9.7: “But, Udāyī, what is that highest splendour than which there is no other splendour higher or more excellent?”
mn79:9.8: “Venerable sir, that splendour than which there is no other splendour higher or more excellent—that is the highest splendour.”
mn79:10.1: “Udāyī, you could go on like this for a long time:
mn79:10.2: ‘That splendour, venerable sir, than which there is no other splendour higher or more excellent—that is the highest splendour’, you say, and yet you do not make known what that splendour is.
mn79:10.3: Suppose, Udāyī, a man were to say thus:
mn79:10.4: ‘I want, I love, the most beautiful girl in this country.’
mn79:10.6: ‘Good man, this most beautiful girl in the country whom you want and love—do you know whether she is a noble lady, or a brahmin lady, or a merchant lady, or a worker’s daughter?’
mn79:10.7: Being asked thus, he would say “No.”
mn79:10.9: ‘Good man, this most beautiful girl in the country whom you want and love—do you know her name and clan, or … whether she is tall or short or of middle height, dark or brown or golden-skinned … or what village or town or city she lives in?’
mn79:10.10: Being asked thus, he would say “No.”
mn79:10.12: ‘Good man, do you then want and love someone you neither know nor see?’
mn79:10.13: Being asked thus, he would say “Yes.”
mn79:10.15: that being so, would not that man’s statement amount to nonsense?”
mn79:10.16: “Certainly, venerable sir, that being so, that man’s statement would amount to nonsense.”
mn79:10.17: “So too, Udāyī, you say: ‘That splendour, venerable sir, than which there is no other splendour higher or more excellent—that is the highest splendour’, and yet you do not make known what that splendour is.”
mn79:11.1: “Venerable sir, just as a beautiful beryl gem of pure water, eight-faceted, well cut, laid on a saffron cloth, gleams, shines, and glows—such is the self, possessed of such splendour, when it is sound after death.”
mn79:12.2: which of these two has the more excellent and superior splendour: a beautiful beryl gem of pure water, eight-faceted, well cut, laid on a saffron cloth, that gleams, shines, and glows, or a glow-worm in the dark of night?”
mn79:12.3: “That glow-worm in the dark of night, venerable sir, has the more excellent and superior splendour of these two.”
mn79:13.2: which of these two has the more excellent and superior splendour: a glow-worm in the dark of night, or an oil lamp in the dark of night?”
mn79:13.3: “That oil lamp in the dark of night, venerable sir, has the more excellent and superior splendour of these two.”
mn79:14.2: which of these two has the more excellent and superior splendour: an oil lamp in the dark of night, or a great bonfire in the dark of night?”
mn79:14.3: “That great bonfire in the dark of night, venerable sir, has the more excellent and superior splendour of these two.”
mn79:15.2: which of these two has the more excellent and superior splendour: a great bonfire in the dark of night, or the morning star at night towards dawn in a clear, cloudless sky?”
mn79:15.3: “That morning star at night towards dawn in a clear, cloudless sky, venerable sir, has the more excellent and superior splendour of these two.”
mn79:16.2: which of these two has the more excellent and superior splendour: the morning star at night towards dawn in a clear, cloudless sky, or the moon at midnight in a clear, cloudless sky on the full-moon Uposatha day of the fifteenth?”
mn79:16.3: “That moon at midnight in a clear, cloudless sky on the full-moon Uposatha day of the fifteenth, venerable sir, has the more excellent and superior splendour of these two.”
mn79:17.2: which of these two has the more excellent and superior splendour: the moon at midnight in a clear, cloudless sky on the full-moon Uposatha day of the fifteenth, or the sun at midday in a clear, cloudless sky in the autumn, in the last month of the rains?”
mn79:17.3: “That sun at midday in a clear, cloudless sky in the autumn, in the last month of the rains, venerable sir, has the more excellent and superior splendour of these two.”
mn79:18.1: “Well, Udāyī, there are far more gods than those who do not partake of the light of the moon and sun—those I know.
mn79:18.3: ‘There is no other splendour higher or more excellent than that.’
mn79:18.4: But you, Udāyī, say that that splendour which is inferior to and worse than a glow-worm’s is the highest splendour, and yet you do not make known what that splendour is.”
mn79:19.1: “The Blessed One has cut off the discussion; the Fortunate One has cut off the discussion.”
mn79:19.3: ‘The Blessed One has cut off the discussion, the Fortunate One has cut off the discussion’?”
mn79:19.4: “Venerable sir, in our own teacher’s doctrine it is thus:
mn79:19.5: ‘This is the highest splendour, this is the highest splendour.’
mn79:19.6: But when we are pressed, questioned, and cross-questioned about our own teacher’s doctrine by the Blessed One, we are found to be empty, hollow, and mistaken.”
mn79:20.1: “But, Udāyī, is there an entirely pleasant world? Is there a definite way to realize that entirely pleasant world?”
mn79:20.2: “Venerable sir, in our own teacher’s doctrine it is thus:
mn79:20.3: ‘There is an entirely pleasant world; there is a definite way to realize that entirely pleasant world.’”
mn79:21.1: “But, Udāyī, what is that definite way to realize the entirely pleasant world?”
mn79:21.2: “Here, venerable sir, someone abandons the killing of living beings and abstains from killing living beings; he abandons taking what is not given and abstains from taking what is not given; he abandons misconduct in sensual desires and abstains from misconduct in sensual desires; he abandons false speech and abstains from false speech; or else he undertakes some form of austerity.
mn79:21.3: This, venerable sir, is that definite way to realize the entirely pleasant world.”
mn79:22.2: on the occasion when one abandons the killing of living beings and abstains from killing living beings, is the self on that occasion entirely happy, or both happy and unhappy?”
mn79:22.5: on the occasion when one abandons taking what is not given and abstains from taking what is not given, is the self on that occasion entirely happy, or both happy and unhappy?”
mn79:22.7: “What do you think, Udāyī, on the occasion when one abandons misconduct in sensual desires and abstains from misconduct in sensual desires, is the self on that occasion entirely happy, or both happy and unhappy?”
mn79:22.9: “What do you think, Udāyī, on the occasion when one abandons false speech and abstains from false speech, is the self on that occasion entirely happy, or both happy and unhappy?”
mn79:22.12: on the occasion when one undertakes some form of austerity, is the self on that occasion entirely happy, or both happy and unhappy?”
mn79:22.15: is the entirely pleasant world realized by following a way mixed with happiness and unhappiness?”
mn79:23.1: “The Blessed One has cut off the discussion; the Fortunate One has cut off the discussion.”
mn79:23.3: ‘The Blessed One has cut off the discussion, the Fortunate One has cut off the discussion’?”
mn79:23.4: “Venerable sir, in our own teacher’s doctrine it is thus:
mn79:23.5: ‘There is an entirely pleasant world; there is a definite way to realize that entirely pleasant world.’
mn79:23.6: But when we are pressed, questioned, and cross-questioned about our own teacher’s doctrine by the Blessed One, we are found to be empty, hollow, and mistaken.
mn79:23.7: But, venerable sir, is there an entirely pleasant world? Is there a definite way to realize that entirely pleasant world?”
mn79:24.1: “There is, Udāyī, an entirely pleasant world; there is a definite way to realize that entirely pleasant world.”
mn79:24.2: “But, venerable sir, what is that definite way to realize the entirely pleasant world?”
mn79:25.1: “Here, Udāyī, quite secluded from sensual desires … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna …
mn79:25.2: with the stilling of initial and sustained application … he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna …
mn79:25.3: with the fading away of joy as well … he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna—
mn79:25.4: this, Udāyī, is that definite way to realize the entirely pleasant world.”
mn79:25.5: “That, venerable sir, is not the way to realize the entirely pleasant world; rather, the entirely pleasant world has already been realized by that point.”
mn79:25.6: “The entirely pleasant world is not yet realized by that point, Udāyī;
mn79:25.7: that is only the definite way to realize the entirely pleasant world.”
mn79:26.1: When this was said, Sakuludāyī the Wanderer’s assembly became loud, noisy, and clamorous:
mn79:26.2: “Here we have lost, along with our teacher’s doctrine! Here we have lost, along with our teacher’s doctrine!
mn79:26.3: We know nothing higher than this.”
mn79:26.4: Then Sakuludāyī the Wanderer, having quieted those wanderers, said to the Blessed One:
mn79:27.1: “But, venerable sir, at what point is the entirely pleasant world realized?”
mn79:27.2: “Here, Udāyī, with the abandoning of pleasure … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna …
mn79:27.3: He consorts, converses, and engages in discussion with those deities who have been reborn in the entirely pleasant world.
mn79:27.4: It is by this point, Udāyī, that the entirely pleasant world is realized.”
mn79:28.1: “Then surely, venerable sir, it is for the sake of realizing this entirely pleasant world that the bhikkhus live the life divine under the Blessed One?”
mn79:28.2: “It is not, Udāyī, for the sake of realizing the entirely pleasant world that the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.
mn79:28.3: There are, Udāyī, other things higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.”
mn79:28.4: “But what, venerable sir, are those things higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under the Blessed One?”
mn79:29-36.1: “Here, Udāyī, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, fully enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed …
mn79:37.1: … having abandoned these five hindrances, defilements of mind that weaken wisdom,
mn79:37.2: quite secluded from sensual desires … he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna …
mn79:37.3: This too, Udāyī, is a thing higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.
mn79:38-40.1: Again, Udāyī, with the stilling of initial and sustained application … the second jhāna …
mn79:38-40.3: he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna.
mn79:38-40.4: This too, Udāyī, is a thing higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.
mn79:41.1: When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of recollection of past lives.
mn79:41.2: He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births … thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.
mn79:41.3: This too, Udāyī, is a thing higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.
mn79:42.1: When his mind is thus concentrated … he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.
mn79:42.2: With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate … he understands how beings pass on according to their actions.
mn79:42.3: This too, Udāyī, is a thing higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.
mn79:43.1: When his mind is thus concentrated … he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of the exhaustion of the taints.
mn79:43.2: He understands as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘this is the origin of suffering’ … ‘this is the cessation of suffering’ … he understands as it actually is: ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’,
mn79:43.3: he understands as it actually is: ‘these are the taints’ … ‘this is the origin of the taints’ … ‘this is the cessation of the taints’ … he understands as it actually is: ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’
mn79:44.1: Knowing and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, liberated from the taint of being, liberated from the taint of ignorance.
mn79:44.2: When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’
mn79:44.3: He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’
mn79:44.4: This too, Udāyī, is a thing higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.
mn79:44.5: These, Udāyī, are the things higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.”
mn79:45.1: When this was said, Sakuludāyī the Wanderer said to the Blessed One:
mn79:45.3: As though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the dark so that those with eyes could see forms—so too the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by the Blessed One.
mn79:45.4: I go to the Blessed One for refuge, venerable sir, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus.
mn79:45.5: I would receive the Going-forth in the Blessed One’s presence, venerable sir, I would receive the Full Admission.”
mn79:46.1: When this was said, Sakuludāyī the Wanderer’s assembly said to Sakuludāyī the Wanderer:
mn79:46.2: “Let not Master Udāyī live the life divine under the ascetic Gotama;
mn79:46.3: let not Master Udāyī, who has been a teacher, live the life of a pupil.
mn79:46.4: Just as a water-jar might become a mere dipper, so it will be for Master Udāyī.[^3]
mn79:46.5: Let not Master Udāyī live the life divine under the ascetic Gotama;
mn79:46.6: let not Master Udāyī, who has been a teacher, live the life of a pupil.”
mn79:46.7: So it was that Sakuludāyī the Wanderer’s assembly obstructed him in living the life divine under the Blessed One.
